Concord Pilot: cost structure, quantization recommendations, and pilot credits

Hi Vanessa,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — ConcordAI is excited about Redwood's streaming and cache behavior. Before we lock the pilot commercials, procurement asked for a simple breakdown: how the proposed pilot credits map to expected token consumption under different quantization settings and batching profiles.

High-level asks from our side: 
- A 6-week pilot for the SearchAssist feature (50k calls/day peak),
- Target SLO: p95 latency <= 250ms,
- We want to understand unit economics: tokens per call (avg/95p), estimated tokens consumed with 8-bit vs 4-bit quant, and expected credits burned with 10/50/100 request batch windows.

Priya and I sketched a short MVP spec (attached). Can you provide a worked example or a simple table so our procurement can sign off? Also single-sentence guidance on the tradeoffs you recommend for ConcordAI's workload (short prompts, long history KV usage).

Samir

attachments: concord_pilot_mvp_spec.pdf (pdf)
Samir — really appreciate the clear ask and the MVP spec. I looped in Aditya (econ) and Marissa (solutions) to give a concise worked example.

Quick overview (attached spreadsheet): we modeled three configurations and show estimated daily credits burned. Key takeaways up front:
- For short prompts with long KV history (your pattern), 8-bit quant gives the best latency/cost balance at pilot scale; 4-bit reduces cost but may increase p95 latency variability for history-heavy calls.
- Batching at the hardware level helps when request concurrency is steady; however, for very low tail-latency targets (<=250ms p95) keep batching small (n<=16) and rely more on KV prefix caching.

Next steps: 1) review the attached proposed_pricing_sheet.xlsx, 2) confirm which config Concord wants us to pilot (we can support 8-bit default + experimental 4-bit variant), 3) I can push a pilot credit commitment for approval with Sales Ops.

I've attached a one-pager (redwood_optimize_onepager.pdf) that summarizes tradeoffs — should help procurement. Happy to jump on a 20-min call to walk through the numbers.

— Vanessa
Vanessa Ortiz
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

attachments: proposed_pricing_sheet.xlsx (xlsx), redwood_optimize_onepager.pdf (pdf)
Hi Samir — quick econ + technical sketch so procurement sees the math. I pulled numbers from our model and the attached sheet. I kept this deliberately compact.

Scenario assumptions (per-call): average prompt+context = 350 tokens, response = 120 tokens, KV cache hits 40% of the time for historical tokens.

Config A — 8-bit (default):
- avg tokens/call: 470
- effective tokens (after cache): 322
- batching profile: 1-16 (typical) -> credits/day @50k calls/day = ~16.1M tokens/day -> pilot credits = 16.1k units (RWD unit = 1000 tokens)
- expected p95 latency: ~180-240ms (meets 250ms)

Config B — 4-bit (aggressive quant):
- avg tokens/call: 470 (same payload)
- effective tokens (after cache): 322
- credits/day reduction: ~32% vs 8-bit -> ~10.9k credits/day
- caveat: p95 latency jitter increases, esp when KV miss and sequence lengths spike; we recommend testing on a small % of traffic first.

Config C — 8-bit + larger batching (burst to 64):
- unit cost improves ~18% vs Config A at steady concurrency, but p95 climbs by ~40-60ms on average; not ideal for strict latency SLO.

Pilot credit ask (6 weeks):
- If Concord wants to run both default 8-bit and 4-bit experiment at 10% traffic, we recommend: 6-week credit pool = 750k credits (~based on 50k calls/day peak, usage curve, and buffer).

If procurement wants a one-line justification for the DocuSign: "Provision pilot credits for a 6-week evaluation covering expected peak consumption with an experimental 4-bit arm (10% traffic)."

Happy to convert any of these numbers to the format your procurement prefers.

— Aditya
Aditya Rao
Pricing & Revenue Operations, Redwood Inference
